content.thinking:
The impact here was really about latency rather than errors, since the error rate stayed flat versus baseline. I shouldn't restate the given figures as if I'd calculated them myself, or introduce any impact numbers of my own — I'll describe the situation without quoting or computing specific metrics.

For the root cause, the monthly-spend-feature flag was enabled and added expensive work to the account page render path, pushing p99 latency from roughly 200ms to over 1700ms. I should flag as assumptions that the ClientDisconnected errors were likely pre-existing and unrelated, that the io-pricing restart may not have actually contributed to recovery, and that the causal link to the flag rollout is based on timing correlation rather than direct code-level proof — also worth noting this flag was implicated in a prior incident where reverting it didn't resolve things, which is why Argus deprioritized it this time.

assumptions: The flag toggle is held to be the cause on timing and elimination — the rollout immediately precedes the latency climb and nothing else changed — rather than on any code-level or profiling evidence that the new feature path is the expensive one.

Dependency latency for io-pricing and io-pay was never actually retrieved; the alternative explanation (a slow downstream call during account-page render) was set aside without direct measurement, and rests only on the fact that restarting io-pricing did not restore the service.

The io-pricing restart is assumed to have had no bearing on recovery. It completed roughly three minutes before the flag was reverted and the service was still off baseline at that point, but a delayed benefit cannot be strictly excluded.

The ClientDisconnected errors on the account page appear before, during and after the incident window and are treated as pre-existing background noise consistent with shoppers abandoning slow or unwanted page loads, not as a symptom of this fault.

This same flag had been reverted on an earlier incident (24dbf726-1ff3-422c-bd31-28e2d6b03179) without the service recovering, which is why it was initially ranked second here. The two incidents are assumed to be unrelated; that has not been verified.
Recovery is judged from the service returning to its latency baseline at the first post-revert check, so the true end of customer impact may sit anywhere between the revert and that check.
input.executive_summary: Between 16:06 and 16:15 UTC on 27 September 2026 (roughly nine minutes), the shop's account pages became very slow to load. Requests still succeeded — the proportion of failing requests stayed at its usual everyday level and did not rise during the incident — so the effect customers would have noticed was waiting, not errors. A newly enabled product feature was responsible: it had been switched on for a small slice of traffic a minute earlier and for all traffic from 16:06, and it made rendering the account page far more expensive. The on-call automation picked up the alert at 16:10, first tried restarting a neighbouring service, which made no difference and was ruled out, then switched the new feature back off at 16:14; the service was confirmed back to its normal speed at 16:15. A draft code change to address the underlying slowness has been opened for review.
input.root_cause: The feature flag `monthly-spend-feature` was turned on for io-shop — a partial rollout is visible in the logs at 16:05 (167 off / 33 on out of 200 evaluations) and fully on from 16:06 — which put additional work on the account-page render path and drove io-shop p99 latency from a ~200ms baseline to over 1700ms, tripping the HighLatency alert. Nothing else in the window changed: no deploy landed, no dependency was shown to be failing, and error rates stayed at their normal level, so this was a latency-only regression attributable to the flag state.
